ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Allentown, PA
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Allentown and Lehigh Valley plants, tanks, piping and steel. Request a quote for your scope.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Allentown, Pennsylvania
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to Allentown and the wider Lehigh Valley for wall-thickness surveys, corrosion mapping by manual scanning, and shear-wave examination of welds on pressure equipment, storage tanks, process piping and structural steel. The work is done at your plant, fabrication shop or yard, under a written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III. To scope a job, use the UT quote request for Allentown and tell us the component, material, nominal thickness and the code that governs it.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Allentown

Allentown sits in a valley whose economy changed shape within one generation. The riverside steel mills that once defined the area are gone, and the former Bethlehem Steel site is now an industrial park and an arts district built around preserved blast furnaces. What replaced the mills is wider than most people expect: truck and cab assembly in Macungie, food and beverage plants along Route 100, pharmaceutical and diagnostic manufacturing, industrial gas and chemical companies, and an enormous volume of warehousing and distribution space along the Route 33 and Interstate 78 corridors. Each of these puts steel in service that eventually needs a thickness reading or a weld examination.

In practical terms, ultrasonic work in the Lehigh Valley falls into a handful of families. Food and beverage plants run steam headers, hot-water loops, ammonia refrigeration receivers and stainless process vessels, and the carbon-steel parts of those systems lose wall to corrosion under insulation and to condensate attack in low points. Industrial gas and chemical sites operate pressure vessels, storage tanks and piping whose inspection plans call for thickness data at fixed condition monitoring locations. Manufacturing plants that fabricate frames, cabs and chassis components weld heavy plate and tube and need volumetric confidence in structural joints. Distribution centers have a quieter need: sprinkler risers, fire-pump piping, compressed-air receivers and the large steel racking and canopy structures that carry building loads.

Older infrastructure matters as well. The Lehigh Valley has a long history of rail, canal and heavy industry, and many facilities reuse tanks, supports and piping that were installed decades ago. When an owner buys or reactivates such a site, an ultrasonic survey is often the fastest way to learn how much steel is left before engineering decides what to repair, derate or replace.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it cannot

Ultrasonic testing sends a sound pulse into a material and times the echo. Two jobs dominate. The first is thickness measurement: the instrument converts the time between the front surface and the back wall into remaining wall, which is what corrosion programs track. The second is weld examination with an angle-beam shear wave probe, which finds planar discontinuities such as lack of fusion, cracks and slag lines that sit inside the weld volume where surface methods cannot reach.

The limits are as important as the capabilities. Sound needs a coupled, reasonably smooth surface, so heavy scale, flaking paint and rough weld caps must be dressed before a trustworthy reading is possible. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic stainless welds scatter and attenuate the beam, which can hide small reflectors and produce misleading noise. Very thin wall and severe pitting are another trap: a probe that sits on the edge of a pit can read the pit floor or a false doubled echo. The technician manages these risks with dual-element probes for corroded surfaces, an A-scan display that lets the operator see the echo pattern instead of trusting a digital number alone, and calibration on a reference block of the same material and similar thickness.

Orientation also matters. A shear-wave beam finds a flaw best when the flaw faces the beam, so a crack running along the weld may need scans from both sides and in more than one skew direction. Where access limits a scan, the report must say so rather than imply full coverage. Our national ultrasonic testing page explains the method in general; this page applies it to Allentown work.

Codes and acceptance criteria used in Pennsylvania

The code decides how a weld is examined and when an indication is rejected, so we ask for it at the start. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, ultrasonic weld examination follows Mandatory Appendix 12, and acceptance of flaws is written there. For process piping under ASME B31.3, ultrasonic examination of welds follows paragraph 344.6 with criteria in Table 341.3.2. Underlying both is ASME Section V: Article 4 governs ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 covers materials, and Article 23 carries the contact pulse-echo thickness practice used on corrosion surveys. Structural groove welds under AWS D1.1 have their own ultrasonic acceptance rules, and state transportation steel is examined to AWS D1.5.

In service, the picture changes. Inspection of vessels, piping and tanks in operating plants follows the owner's inspection program, often built on API 510, API 570 and API 653. Under those codes the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and the integrity decision. Atlantis does not act as that inspector; we perform the ultrasonic examination, record the data and hand it to the inspector. Thickness practice also references ASTM E797 for contact measurement. For a plain-language primer, see our guide to ASME Section V Article 5 thickness measurement requirements.

Pennsylvania has its own regime for pressure equipment. The Department of Labor and Industry's Boiler Division administers the state's boiler and unfired pressure vessel rules, and periodic inspections are performed by inspectors who hold a Pennsylvania commission, either state staff or insurance company inspectors. According to the department's published summary, unfired pressure vessels are inspected at 36-month intervals, a certificate of operation is issued from the inspector's report, and repairs or alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, with welded repair work limited to organizations that hold an R stamp. Our thickness and weld data feeds into those programs; it does not replace the commissioned inspector's role.

How the work is done: thickness surveys

A thickness survey starts with a map. The owner or inspector marks condition monitoring locations on a drawing or isometric, and we read the same spots each cycle so the corrosion rate is meaningful. The technician prepares each spot by removing loose scale and paint, applies couplant, and calibrates the instrument on a step block made of the same material across the expected thickness range. On corroded carbon steel a dual-element probe is the usual choice because it separates transmit and receive paths and copes better with rough, pitted metal. The A-scan is watched, not just the number, so a doubled echo or a lamination reading is recognized as such.

Hot service needs extra care. Steam lines and hot process piping change sound velocity with temperature, so readings are corrected, and high-temperature probes and couplant are used where the surface is too hot for standard materials. The report records surface temperature so the engineer can interpret the figures. For tanks, readings are commonly taken on a grid on shell courses and at the bottom edge, and each reading is logged against its grid cell. When a location reads below an alarm level the technician flags it immediately to the inspector, so a follow-up scan can define the extent of metal loss before anyone leaves the area.

How the work is done: ultrasonic weld examination

Weld examination uses angle-beam probes, typically 45, 60 and 70 degrees, chosen to suit thickness and joint geometry. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, and indications are measured against it. The technician scans along and across the weld from the accessible sides, records the position, length and amplitude of anything that exceeds the recording level, and evaluates it against the construction code. Because shear-wave work depends on interpretation, it is performed only by a qualified Level II or above, and the written procedure is approved by the Level III before the job starts.

Surface condition on the weld cap and adjacent base metal decides whether scans can be completed. Welds left with high crowns or spatter may need grinding. When welds are in the field, such as erected tank shells or structural joints, we plan access, lighting and scaffolding with your supervisor so the scan is complete and safe.

Who does the work and how they are qualified

Atlantis has no office in Allentown. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and travel to your plant, shop or yard. They are qualified under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. In that scheme the employer certifies its own personnel: a Level II sets up and calibrates equipment, performs the examination and interprets results, and an ASNT Level III establishes techniques, approves procedures and reviews reports. Certification of your own staff remains your decision as the employer, and our qualification does not replace a site's own requirements; if your contract needs specific qualification wording, tell us when you request the quote.

What the ultrasonic report contains

A usable report lets an engineer or inspector reproduce the job. Ours identifies the component and the location of each reading, the procedure number and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block used, the technician and certification level, and the surface temperature where relevant. For thickness work the report presents a table or a grid of readings against nominal and minimum required wall. For welds it lists each indication with position, length, depth and amplitude relative to the reference level, followed by a clear accept or reject against the named criteria, with sketches to show where the indication sits. Data is delivered in the format your inspection database expects wherever possible.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Allentown

Lehigh Valley weather shapes the schedule. Winters bring freezing surfaces that thicken couplant, slow instrument displays and complicate calibration, so outdoor tanks and yard piping may call for heated couplant or waiting for a milder window. Summer sun can push exposed steel above the comfortable limit for standard probes, which is where high-temperature probes and cooling breaks come in. Outages at manufacturing sites usually follow production calendars, so early planning avoids a collision with other contractors working the same shutdown.

Logistics also vary. Plants along Route 100 and the industrial parks off Route 33 often require site-specific safety orientation, badging and permits before technicians can enter, so give us your requirements early. Interstate 78 makes travel straightforward, but heavy truck traffic around distribution hubs can affect arrival planning; we agree timing with your supervisor rather than promising an arrival window. Tell us whether the equipment is in service, and whether hot work or confined-space entry is involved, because both change how a scan is staged.

UT, MT or PT: choosing the right method in Allentown

Ultrasonic testing answers volume and wall questions: how thick is the steel and is there a planar flaw inside the weld. It is the right tool for corrosion surveys and for welds where internal fusion matters. If your question is whether a weld toe or a fillet has a surface crack in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Allentown is faster and more sensitive to surface breaking cracks. If the material is stainless steel or aluminum, liquid penetrant testing in Allentown detects surface-breaking flaws on non-magnetic metals. Many jobs combine methods: UT to confirm remaining wall after a leak, then PT or MT to confirm that a repair weld is free of surface defects. For state-level context see our Pennsylvania inspection services page.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Some Allentown plants prefer to build in-house capability. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training with a Level III instructor, practice on the ultrasonic testing simulator, and a path to qualification under your own written practice. See the NDT training page for Allentown for how delivery works for employers in the Lehigh Valley. If you need a written practice or procedures drafted first, our Level III consulting can help.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing involve at an Allentown plant?
faq.a: A technician cleans selected spots, applies couplant, calibrates on a step block of matching material and reads remaining wall at marked condition monitoring locations. Results are logged against nominal and minimum thickness so your inspector can track corrosion rate over time.

faq.q: Can you examine welds ultrasonically as well as measure thickness?
faq.a: Yes. Level II technicians use angle-beam shear wave probes and a reference curve to examine groove welds for lack of fusion, cracks and slag, then evaluate indications against the construction code you name, such as ASME Section VIII, B31.3 or AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Do you inspect the vessels and tanks on behalf of the state of Pennsylvania?
faq.a: No. Pennsylvania boiler and unfired pressure vessel inspections are carried out by commissioned inspectors under the Department of Labor and Industry's rules. We perform the ultrasonic examination and give your inspector the data to use in their own work.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing work on stainless steel and cast parts?
faq.a: It can, but coarse grain and austenitic weld structure scatter the sound beam, so sensitivity and reliability drop. We discuss the material up front and may propose reference blocks of the same alloy or a different method if the part is a poor candidate.

faq.q: How should surfaces be prepared before ultrasonic inspection?
faq.a: Remove loose scale, flaking paint and weld spatter at the inspection spots, and grind high weld caps where angle-beam scanning is planned. A smooth, clean surface lets couplant transmit sound reliably and prevents false or unreadable echoes.

faq.q: What information do you need to quote an ultrasonic job in the Lehigh Valley?
faq.a: Send the component type, material, nominal thickness, governing code, approximate number of locations or weld length, access conditions, and whether equipment is in service. Add site safety requirements so we plan the mobilization properly. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Who qualifies your ultrasonic technicians?
faq.a: Technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II personnel perform and interpret the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. If your contract specifies other qualification wording, tell us before the job.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a weld?
faq.a: That depends on the construction code and the owner's agreement. Some codes include ultrasonic provisions for production welds, but the substitution must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before work starts.

faq.q: Can you train our maintenance staff in ultrasonic thickness gauging?
faq.a: Yes. We offer UT Level 1 and Level 2 courses and simulator practice, and can help you set up the written practice under which your employer qualifies and certifies its own technicians following SNT-TC-1A.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Allentown, PA | MT
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing of welds, cranes, rigging and steel structures in Allentown and the Lehigh Valley. Quote online.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Allentown, Pennsylvania
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Allentown and the surrounding Lehigh Valley to perform magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) on carbon and low-alloy steel welds, castings, forgings, crane components and structural connections. Yoke and prod techniques with dry or wet particles locate surface and near-surface cracks that a visual check can miss. Use the MT quote request for Allentown and tell us the part, the material, the code and how many welds or components are involved.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Allentown

Allentown is a region of steel fabrication and heavy handling. Truck cab and chassis assembly in nearby Macungie, machine shops and metal fabricators, and food and beverage plants with large frames and supports all rely on welded carbon steel. The area also carries the memory of Bethlehem Steel, and the people who work in its industrial parks understand that fatigue cracks start at welds and sharp changes of section. Today the largest consumer of steel by footprint is warehousing: the Route 33 and Interstate 78 corridors are lined with distribution buildings whose rooftop frames, loading-dock equipment, forklift masts and overhead cranes see repeated loading.

Typical MT targets in this setting include weld toes on structural frames, lifting lugs and padeyes, crane hooks and hoist structures, truck frame cross members, pressure vessel nozzle welds in carbon steel, support lugs on tanks and receivers, shafts and gears in plant machinery, and hydraulic cylinder components. Because many of these parts cycle in load, the cracks MT is built to find are fatigue cracks, which begin at the surface and grow slowly until a part fails suddenly. Finding them while they are tight and short is the difference between a repair and a replacement.

The region also has an aging stock of industrial buildings and equipment that new owners are putting back into service. A pre-use MT survey of lifting points and structural welds is a straightforward way to establish a baseline before a hoist or a platform returns to work.

What magnetic particle inspection finds and what it misses

MT works because a crack in magnetized ferromagnetic steel disturbs the magnetic field and forms a small leakage field that attracts fine iron particles. The particles gather along the crack and make it visible. It detects surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities in material that can be magnetized: carbon steel and most low-alloy steels. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or other non-magnetic metals, so a stainless fabrication in a dairy or beverage line calls for a different method.

The technique is directional. The field must cross the crack at a favorable angle, so we examine each area twice with the field direction turned roughly ninety degrees, to reveal cracks running in any direction. MT also has depth limits: it is strong on tight surface cracks but weak on buried flaws. Heavy paint, scale or rust reduces sensitivity, and very rough surfaces can hold particles and create false indications that must be sorted into relevant and non-relevant. When the work calls for confirmation of volumetric quality, ultrasonic testing in Allentown complements MT. For a general overview, read our complete guide to magnetic particle testing or visit the national magnetic particle testing page.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply

MT is performed to a written procedure that follows the construction or service code. ASME Section V Article 7 sets out the method requirements: yoke lifting power, field strength verification, particle types, lighting and examination coverage. Acceptance is then taken from the code that governs the item. For ASME Section VIII Division 1 vessels, Mandatory Appendix 6 contains MT methods and acceptance. ASME B31.3 piping calls for MT under paragraph 344.3 with criteria in Table 341.3.2. Structural steel welded to AWS D1.1 has visual and magnetic particle provisions in its inspection clause, and state bridge steel follows AWS D1.5. ASTM E709 is a guide to MT and ASTM E1444 is the practice covering the method in general industry. Our explainer on ASME Section V Article 7 walks through the main requirements.

The state layer matters for pressure equipment. Pennsylvania's Department of Labor and Industry runs the Boiler Division, which issues operating certificates for boilers and unfired pressure vessels based on inspections by commissioned inspectors. When welding repairs are carried out on a vessel, the National Board Inspection Code governs the repair, and welded repairs are limited to organizations holding an R stamp. MT after repair welding is a routine acceptance step. Atlantis performs the MT and reports the indications; the commissioned inspector and the repair organization remain responsible for their own roles.

Technique: yokes, prods and particles

Most field MT in Allentown is done with a portable electromagnetic yoke, which magnetizes the area between its legs. Under Article 7, an alternating-current yoke must demonstrate a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. We check the yoke with a test weight before use and on the schedule your procedure sets. Prods can be used for large castings or heavy welds where a yoke cannot reach, but prods carry a risk of arc burns at the contact points, so they are avoided on finished surfaces and heat-sensitive alloys.

Particles come in two broad families. Dry powder is common on rough welds and in hot or outdoor conditions, and suits yoke work in the field. Wet suspension, usually fluorescent, is more sensitive for fine cracks and is the usual choice on machined components or critical welds. Fluorescent examination takes place under UV-A light in a darkened area, so we plan for a shaded setup or an enclosure. Visible-color particles used with a white contrast paint are an alternative where darkness is hard to achieve.

Demagnetization follows when residual magnetism could interfere with later operations. Residual fields can disturb arc welding, attract chips on a machined part or upset bearings and instruments, so the procedure states whether demagnetization is needed and how the field is checked afterward. Parts are cleaned of particles before they return to service.

Fatigue, lifting equipment and why surface cracks matter

Lifting gear deserves its own mention because the consequences of failure are severe. Hooks, shackles, spreader beams, hoist frames and runway girders carry load cycles every shift, and the cracks that grow in them are almost always surface-initiated. Owners of cranes and below-the-hook devices often schedule periodic MT as part of their frequent and periodic inspection routines, with the scope and acceptance written by the responsible engineer. We perform the examination to your procedure, report every indication and leave the decision on removal from service with you.

Surface preparation and indication evaluation

Good results start with clean steel. Oil, grease, loose scale and heavy paint must be removed in the inspection area, and welds left rough may need light grinding. The technician evaluates every indication: a linear indication from a crack, a rounded indication from porosity, and the many non-relevant indications that come from magnetic writing, changes in section or the edge of a weld. Relevant indications are measured and compared against the code's acceptance criteria. Disputed indications may be wiped away and re-tested to confirm whether they reappear.

Coverage, lighting and verification

A magnetic particle examination is only as good as its coverage. The procedure defines overlap between yoke positions, the area examined around each weld, and the lighting at the surface, which for visible particles must be bright enough to see fine lines and for fluorescent work must be matched with low ambient light. Before the job we confirm the particles are performing, using a known reference or a pie-shaped field indicator that shows the field direction in the part. Where a result is doubtful, the area is re-examined rather than accepted on a hunch.

Who performs the inspection

Atlantis has no office in Allentown. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, fabrication shop or yard for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which the employer certifies its own personnel. A Level II sets up the equipment and performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. If your owner specification requires different qualification evidence, we discuss it before the quote, not after the work.

What the MT report contains

The report names the component and each examined area, the procedure number and revision, the technique and current or yoke type, the particles and carrier, and the lighting used. It records equipment checks such as yoke lifting power, the technician's name and certification level, the date and the surface condition. Each indication is listed with location, orientation and length, with an accept or reject decision against the named criteria, and sketches or photographs mark where it sits. A clear record of areas examined with no indications is as valuable as the defects, because it proves coverage.

Planning an MT job in Allentown

Weather is the main variable. In cold months, steel temperatures drop and wet suspension carriers become sluggish, so outdoor work such as crane runways and yard structures may need procedures that cover low temperatures or a delay for a milder day. Summer heat can push exposed steel too hot for wet methods, which is where dry powder and shaded setups help. Humidity and rain complicate yard work, so a covered area makes a difference.

Access is a second factor. Overhead cranes, roof frames and elevated platforms need lift equipment or scaffolds and fall protection arranged with your safety lead. Many plants in the industrial parks along Route 33 and Route 100 require orientation and permits before contractors enter. Share your site rules with us early. We coordinate timing with your supervisor and do not promise an arrival window in advance.

MT, PT or UT: choosing the right method in Allentown

For surface cracks in carbon or low-alloy steel, MT is usually the fastest and most sensitive field method. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or a non-magnetic alloy, use liquid penetrant testing in Allentown instead. When the concern is wall loss or an internal flaw in a weld, choose ultrasonic testing, covered on our Allentown UT page. If you are comparing the two surface methods, our MT versus PT comparison explains where each wins. For Pennsylvania-wide scopes, see inspection services in Pennsylvania.

Training your own MT technicians

Plants that want to build in-house capability can start with MT Level 1 training and move to MT Level 2 training, both led by an ASNT Level III. The training page for Allentown explains how courses reach employers in the Lehigh Valley, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows the experience and hours your technicians will need under your written practice.

faq.q: What materials can be inspected with magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: MT works only on ferromagnetic materials such as carbon steel and most low-alloy steels. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper cannot be magnetized, so those parts need liquid penetrant testing or another method instead.

faq.q: What kinds of defects does magnetic particle inspection detect in Allentown steel structures?
faq.a: It finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks, laps, seams and lack of fusion at weld toes and edges. Fatigue cracks at crane lugs, frame welds and shafts are common targets because they start at the surface.

faq.q: Why do you test each area in two directions?
faq.a: A crack is detected best when the magnetic field crosses it at a right angle. Examining each area twice with the field turned about ninety degrees ensures cracks running in any direction produce a visible indication.

faq.q: Should we use dry powder or wet fluorescent particles?
faq.a: Dry powder suits rough welds, outdoor work and hot surfaces. Wet fluorescent suspension is more sensitive for fine cracks on machined or critical parts, but needs a darkened area for the UV-A examination. We choose based on your procedure and site.

faq.q: Is demagnetization required after MT?
faq.a: Only when residual magnetism could interfere with welding, machining, bearings or instruments. The written procedure states the requirement, and we check the remaining field afterward when demagnetization is called for.

faq.q: Can MT be done through paint or coating?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings may be acceptable if the procedure is qualified for them, but heavy paint, scale and rust reduce sensitivity. We discuss coating thickness and condition when you request a quote and remove coating where required.

faq.q: How do I request MT inspection for a plant near Allentown?
faq.a: Send the component or weld type, material, governing code, quantity, access conditions and any site safety requirements through the quote form. Atlantis mobilizes technicians to your site for the agreed scope, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Are your MT technicians certified by Atlantis to work under my company's rules?
faq.a: Atlantis qualifies its technicians under its written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, where the employer certifies. If your owner specification names different requirements, tell us up front so we can confirm what documentation you need.

faq.q: Can your team train our employees to do MT themselves?
faq.a: Yes. We offer MT Level 1 and Level 2 training with an ASNT Level III instructor, and our Level III consulting can help you write the procedures and written practice your company will use to qualify its own technicians.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | Allentown, PA
pt.description: On-site dye penetrant inspection (PT) of stainless, aluminum and carbon steel welds and castings in Allentown and the Lehigh Valley. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Allentown, Pennsylvania
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Allentown and the Lehigh Valley to carry out liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection or PT, on welds, castings, machined parts and fabricated equipment. PT shows cracks, laps, porosity and pinholes that break the surface of any non-porous metal, which makes it the go-to method for stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic alloys. Tell us what you need through the PT quote request for Allentown, including the material, surface finish and governing code.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Allentown

The Lehigh Valley has a large base of food, beverage, pharmaceutical and diagnostic manufacturing, and these industries run on stainless steel. Hygienic process piping, jacketed mixing vessels, heat exchangers, tank welds and clean-in-place systems are all built from austenitic stainless steel, which cannot be examined by magnetic particle methods. A crack at a tank seam or a pinhole in a tube weld can be a product-safety problem as well as a mechanical one, so penetrant examination of repair and fabrication welds is a routine quality step in these facilities.

Other uses follow the area's industrial mix. Machine shops and metal fabricators produce aluminum and stainless components that need a surface check before shipment. Industrial gas and chemical sites operate vessels, tubing and valves in alloys where PT is the practical surface method. Truck and heavy equipment manufacturing uses PT on aluminum fittings, castings and non-magnetic parts. Warehouses and distribution centers add mechanical equipment: refrigeration systems, air receivers, brazed and welded fittings and stainless sanitary lines in cold-storage buildings.

The older industrial legacy of the valley still matters. Reactivated plants often contain mixed alloys of unknown condition. A penetrant check of accessible welds and repairs gives owners an early read on whether surface cracking is present before they commit to restart.

What penetrant testing finds and what it cannot

PT relies on capillary action. A low-viscosity penetrant is applied to a clean surface, left to dwell, then removed from the surface so that only the liquid trapped inside discontinuities remains. A developer draws that liquid out and spreads it into a visible indication. The method detects only flaws that are open to the surface. It will not find subsurface cracks, lack of fusion buried in a weld, or wall loss, and a crack that has been smeared closed by grinding, shot blasting or machining may not hold penetrant at all. For this reason, cleaning and surface preparation are the center of the method.

PT works on almost any non-porous material: carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, and many ceramics and plastics. Porous surfaces such as unsealed castings or rough, absorbent coatings trap penetrant everywhere and obscure indications. Over-washing can remove penetrant from shallow cracks, and under-washing leaves a background that hides them. When the concern is internal, we recommend ultrasonic testing in Allentown; for surface cracks in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Allentown is often faster. For fundamentals see our national liquid penetrant testing page.

Codes and acceptance criteria used with PT

The written procedure follows the governing code. ASME Section V Article 6 sets the requirements for penetrant materials, process times, surface preparation, temperature and evaluation. Acceptance criteria then come from the construction or service code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.6 for structural and stainless welds. ASTM E165 is the standard practice for penetrant examination in general industry, and it is often referenced in owner specifications. A deeper read is available in our guide to ASME Section V Article 6.

For pressure equipment, Pennsylvania's Boiler Division, part of the Department of Labor and Industry, regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels, and inspections are performed by commissioned inspectors. Repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code and must be performed by organizations holding an R stamp. After weld repair on stainless vessels, PT is the usual surface check. Atlantis performs the PT and records the indications; the commissioned inspector decides what the result means for the vessel's certificate.

Facilities in food and pharmaceutical production often layer customer or quality-system requirements on top of code, such as surface finish and cleanability expectations. Tell us which documents apply so the procedure and the report match them.

Technique: penetrant type, removal and development

Penetrants are classified by dye and removal method. Type I uses fluorescent dye viewed under UV-A light, and Type II uses visible red dye viewed in white light. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and suits critical welds and fine cracks, but needs a darkened viewing area. Visible dye is the workhorse of field PT because no darkness is needed. Removal is classified as water-washable, post-emulsifiable, or solvent-removable. Solvent-removable systems dominate field work on welds because they need no running water and offer controlled cleaning with lint-free wipes dampened with solvent.

The sequence is consistent. Clean the area and let solvent flash off. Apply penetrant and hold for the dwell time in the procedure. Remove the excess carefully so that surface background is gone but entrapped penetrant is not. Apply developer, which can be dry powder, water-suspended or a non-aqueous wet suspension, and allow development time before the final evaluation. A trained technician interprets indications, separating cracks and linear flaws from rounded porosity and from false indications caused by scratches, weld spatter or incomplete cleaning. Comparator blocks and system checks confirm that the materials are performing before the job.

Temperature, cleanliness and compatibility

Temperature has a direct effect on penetrant performance. Article 6 treats a band of roughly 5 to 52 degrees Celsius as the standard range for the part and the materials; working outside that band means the procedure must be qualified for the temperature that will actually be used. Lehigh Valley winters can drop outdoor steel well below the range, and summer sun can raise it above, so exterior tanks and yard piping need planning around the weather or a procedure qualified for the conditions.

Compatibility is an issue on special alloys. For stainless steel, nickel alloys and titanium, penetrant materials are controlled for halogen and sulfur content, because residues can promote cracking in service. Food and pharmaceutical customers also need all penetrant, developer and solvent removed afterward so the surface is clean before the equipment returns to product contact. The post-clean step is written into the procedure and noted in the report.

Welds, repairs and the moment PT earns its keep

Most penetrant work in a plant is tied to a weld event. After a repair, a technician grinds out the defect, welds, dresses the surface and calls for PT at the cavity and again on the finished weld. A root pass on critical stainless piping may be examined before it is covered by fill passes, because a crack found at that stage costs minutes to fix, while the same crack found after hydrotesting costs days. Tell us when you plan these hold points so the examination fits the welding sequence rather than delaying it.

Reading a penetrant indication correctly

Interpretation is the skill that separates a useful PT report from a messy one. A crack bleeds out as a sharp, continuous line that grows slowly as more penetrant emerges. Porosity appears as scattered round dots, and a lack of fusion at a weld edge shows as an intermittent line. Scratches, tool marks and wiping streaks can mimic these, and the technician wipes a suspect indication and reapplies developer to see whether it returns in the same place and form. We record both the relevant indications and the ones we dismissed, with the reason, so your reviewer can follow the logic.

They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which means the employer certifies its own personnel. If your quality system calls for particular qualification evidence, ask when you request the quote.

What the PT report contains

A PT report documents the component, the area examined, the procedure number and revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by type and batch, the dwell and development times, the surface temperature, the technician and certification level, and the examination date. Each indication is described by location, type, size and orientation, then judged against the named acceptance criteria. Photographs or sketches show where indications sit, and a note records that surfaces were post-cleaned where required. Areas with no indications are listed too, so that coverage is clear.

Planning a PT job in Allentown

PT is sensitive to the environment. Cold surfaces slow capillary action and thicken solvents, and heat can flash penetrant off before it has dwelled. Wind and dust carry debris onto freshly cleaned surfaces, so outdoor work benefits from windbreaks or a covered bay. Where we need darkness for fluorescent examination, a tent or a dim room has to be arranged in advance.

Food and pharmaceutical plants usually have strict rules for contractors: gowning, hygiene, allergen controls and tool inspection before anything enters production areas. Tell us about these needs early, because consumables must be approved by quality staff and sometimes must be documented as food-safe or low-residue. Industrial parks off Route 33 and along Route 100 often have orientation and permit processes. We agree timing with your supervisor, and we do not promise an arrival window in advance.

PT, MT or UT: choosing the right method in Allentown

Use PT when the part is non-magnetic or the surface is machined or finished, when you need to check a stainless weld, or when the shape makes magnetization impractical. Use MT for carbon steel when speed and sensitivity to surface-breaking cracks matter. Choose UT when the question is thickness or internal weld quality. faq.q: Is dye penetrant inspection a different method from liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: No, the two names describe one method. Liquid penetrant testing (PT) is the formal term, while dye penetrant inspection is the everyday shop name for the visible or fluorescent dye process that reveals surface-breaking flaws.

faq.q: Which materials can PT inspect in Allentown plants?
faq.a: PT works on almost any non-porous material, including carbon and stainless steel, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys. It is the practical choice for non-magnetic alloys common in food, beverage and pharmaceutical process equipment.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks beneath the surface?
faq.a: No. PT detects only discontinuities open to the surface. Buried lack of fusion, internal cracks and wall loss need ultrasonic testing or another volumetric method, and surface smearing from grinding can hide shallow cracks.

faq.q: How important is cleaning before penetrant testing?
faq.a: Cleaning is critical. Oil, paint, scale and smeared metal block penetrant from entering cracks, so the area is cleaned and allowed to dry before application. Poor preparation is the most common cause of missed indications.

faq.q: Can PT be performed in cold weather?
faq.a: Standard procedures cover a defined temperature band. Colder or hotter surfaces need a procedure qualified for that temperature or a change in schedule, because temperature affects how penetrant behaves and how developer performs.

faq.q: Do you control penetrant materials for stainless steel work?
faq.a: Yes. For stainless steel, nickel alloys and titanium we use materials controlled for halogen and sulfur content when the specification requires it, and we remove all residues so surfaces are clean before equipment returns to service.

faq.a: Atlantis qualifies technicians under its written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II personnel perform and interpret the examination and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Tell us if your quality system needs additional evidence.
